topic: Getting more Google enquiries without ads
title: How can a tradesman get more enquiries from Google without paying for ads?
metaTitle: Get More Google Enquiries Without Ads
description: A practical guide for tradespeople: the free things that bring in more enquiries from Google, in the order worth doing them.
card: The free, practical steps that bring more enquiries from Google, in the order a tradesperson should do them.
summary: Get your Google Business Profile complete and accurate, collect reviews steadily, and give every service and every town you cover its own clear page on a fast website. Then make it easy to call or message, and reply quickly. None of it costs ad money, but it does take some time. It builds up slowly and keeps working once it is in place.

sections.heading: Where free Google enquiries actually come from
paragraphs: When someone searches for a roofer, a builder or a driveway firm near them, Google usually shows two things. At the top is a map with a short list of local firms. Below it are ordinary website results. Free enquiries come from appearing in one or both of those, for the work you want and the places you cover.

They work a bit differently, so it helps to treat them as two jobs. The map list is driven mostly by your Google Business Profile, your reviews and how close you are to the searcher. The website results are driven by whether your site has a clear page that answers what the person searched for, and whether it loads quickly on a phone.

sections.heading: Step one: sort out your Google Business Profile
paragraphs: This is the best place to start because it is free, it is quick, and many trade firms have only half done it. Claim your profile, choose the right main category for what you actually do, and add the other services you offer. Put in your real service area rather than leaving it vague, and make sure your phone number and opening hours are right.

Then add real photos of your own work. Photos of finished jobs, taken on site, do more than stock images ever will. We cover the whole process in the guide to [Google Business Profile for tradesmen](/guides/google-business-profile-for-tradesmen).

bullets.text: your name, address and phone number should match across your profile, your website and any directories you are on.
a driveway firm listed as a general builder confuses Google and customers alike.
add new photos after jobs and answer any questions that come in.

sections.heading: Step two: collect reviews steadily
paragraphs: Reviews help you show up and help people choose you once they have found you. Two firms can sit side by side on the map, and the one with recent, specific reviews tends to get the call.

The trick is to ask at the right moment, which is when the customer is pleased and the job is fresh. Send a short message with a direct link, and ask while you are still on site or that same evening. A steady trickle looks better than a burst once a year. There is a full walkthrough in [how to get more Google reviews](/guides/how-to-get-more-google-reviews).
Reply to every review, good or bad, in a calm and polite way. Future customers read the replies as much as the reviews.

sections.heading: Step three: give each service and town its own page
paragraphs: This is where most trade websites fall down. A single page that says "roofing, extensions, driveways, landscaping, all areas" gives Google very little to work with. Someone searching for a flat roof repair in a particular town wants a page that is clearly about exactly that.

Aim for one page per main service, written in plain words about what you do and how you do it. Then add a page covering the areas you work in, naming the towns and villages honestly. Only list places you would actually travel to. If you take on a lot of work in one particular town, a page for that town is worth having, as long as it says something real rather than repeating the same text with a different place name.

If you want an idea of how this looks for your trade, the pages on websites for [roofers](/websites-for/roofers), [driveway installers](/websites-for/driveway-installers) and [landscapers](/websites-for/landscapers) show how a trade site can be laid out around the work people actually search for.

sections.heading: Step four: show real jobs, not just claims
paragraphs: Google and customers both respond to proof. After a job, write a few short paragraphs about it: what the customer had, what you did, what materials you used, roughly how long it took and which town it was in. Add a few of your own photos. Do not use customer names or addresses without asking.

Over time these write-ups build into a library of evidence that you do the work in the places you want more of. They also give you natural wording that matches how people search, because you are describing real jobs in plain language.
Keep each write-up honest. If a job had a snag and you handled it well, say so. That reads as trustworthy.

bullets.text: a leaking valley, a tired drive, a loft that needed more room.
the method and materials, in words a customer would use.
the town or area, not the full address.
your own, taken in decent light.

sections.heading: Step five: make the site fast and easy on a phone
paragraphs: Most people searching for a tradesperson are on their phone, often while standing in the problem. If your page takes too long to appear, they go back and try the next firm on the list. Speed is also something Google takes into account, so it affects both who finds you and who stays.

You can check your own site for free with the [speed test](/speed-test). If the mobile result is poor, the usual culprits are huge photos, heavy page-builder code and too many add-ons. Resizing and compressing your images is often the quickest fix you can do yourself.

Check the basics on your own phone too. Can you tap to call from the top of every page? Can you read the text without zooming? Does the enquiry form work and is it short? If any answer is no, fix that before anything else.

sections.heading: Step six: make it easy to enquire, then reply fast
paragraphs: Getting found is only half the job. Put your phone number, a WhatsApp link and a short enquiry form where people can see them without scrolling around. Ask only for what you need: name, number, what the job is and where.

Then reply quickly. A person who has sent several enquiries will often go with whoever gets back to them first and sounds sensible. Set up a notification so a new enquiry reaches your phone straight away, and if you are on a roof all day, a short automatic reply saying when you will call back is better than silence.

If you are getting visitors but no enquiries, the cause is usually on the site itself. The guide on a [website not getting enquiries](/guides/website-not-getting-enquiries) goes through what to check.

sections.heading: What to skip
paragraphs: Some things are not worth your time or money. Be wary of anyone who promises a place at the top of Google for a monthly fee, or who sells you bundles of links. Stuffing your page with the same phrase over and over does not help and makes the text hard to read. Copying text from another firm's site does not help either.

Directories can be worth a look for the extra visibility, but they should support your own site, not replace it. If you are weighing that up, see [Checkatrade or your own website](/guides/checkatrade-or-your-own-website).

sections.heading: A sensible order to do it in
paragraphs: If you only have a spare hour or two a week, work through it in this order: complete your Google Business Profile, start asking every happy customer for a review, check your site on your phone and fix anything slow or awkward, then add a page for each service and your areas. After that, write up one finished job at a time.

None of this is quick. Local results build over months rather than days, but each piece stays in place and keeps working. If you would rather hand the website side to someone, the [prices and what's included](/work) page shows how that works with Scalar Digital, and you can [get in touch](/contact) with any questions.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get more enquiries from Google without ads?
faqs.a: It varies with your area and how much competition there is. A completed Business Profile and new reviews can make a difference fairly soon, but website pages usually take longer to build up. Expect it to be a matter of months, not days.

faqs.q: Do I need a website, or is a Google Business Profile enough?
faqs.a: A profile alone can bring calls, but a website gives you room to explain each service, show your jobs and cover the towns you work in. The two work best together. See [is a website worth it for tradesmen](/guides/is-a-website-worth-it-for-tradesmen) for more.

faqs.q: Should I list every town I cover on my website?
faqs.a: List the places you would genuinely travel to for work, and give extra detail for the ones you want more jobs in. Long lists of towns you never visit make the page look thin and do not help.

faqs.q: Can I do all of this myself?
faqs.a: Yes. Most of it is time rather than technical skill: profile, reviews, photos and job write-ups. The part people often hand over is building a fast site, since slow, bloated pages hold the rest back.
